precepts.text: Hannah vowed a vow: give unto thine handmaid a man child, and I will give him unto the Lord all the days of his life; the pattern of a singular vow.
precepts.point: Christ taught on this because a vow is dangerous: you must pay your vow. Better not to swear at all, but let your communication be yea, yea; that is why we just say Lord's will, Lord's will I get this done.
precepts.why:
Hannah is the pattern of a singular vow. A singular vow is a man binding himself to the Most High: promising that in exchange for a blessing he will give himself, or what is his, to the service of the Lord.

Hannah “was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the Lord, and wept sore. And she vowed a vow, and said, O Lord of hosts, if thou wilt indeed look on the affliction of thine handmaid, and remember me, and not forget thine handmaid, but wilt give unto thine handmaid a man child, then I will give him unto the Lord all the days of his life, and there shall no razor come upon his head.”

The blessing asked was a man child; the thing vowed was the child himself, a person given for the Lord, as Leviticus 27 speaks of the persons being for the Lord. That is how the story of Samuel began.

precepts.text: Perform unto the Lord thine oaths; but swear not at all, and let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay.
precepts.point: Christ taught on this because a vow is dangerous: you must pay your vow. Better not to swear at all, but let your communication be yea, yea; that is why we just say Lord's will, Lord's will I get this done.
precepts.why:
Christ taught on this because a vow is dangerous: you must pay your vow. He said, “ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths”.

“But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.”

Better not to swear at all: “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” That is why we just say Lord’s will, Lord’s will I get this done.

precepts.text: When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the Lord by thy estimation; the law already valued what was vowed.
precepts.point: If thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee; but that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform. Do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.why:
“If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word.” A vow is promising the Lord you will do a thing. The law already dealt with vows before Numbers 30: “When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the Lord by thy estimation.”

What was vowed was valued by the priest’s estimation. The law already put a price on what a man vowed, so a vow was never a light word; it was something the Lord counted and required.

precepts.text: When we bring tithes, which is food, to Jerusalem, you give the tenth part that the Lord blessed you with; that tenth part is the mercy that He shows us.
precepts.point: Rain also comes for the land's sake; the land needs to be watered, vegetation needs to grow. And waters and rain also come for mercy's sake.

note.label: Job 37: The Works of the Most High

precepts.why:
“He causeth it to come, whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy.” The flood during Noah's time came for correction; the rain and the hail around Egypt's time came for correction. Rain also comes for the land's sake, because the land needs to be watered and vegetation needs to grow. And waters and rain also come for mercy's sake.

“And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the Lord’s: it is holy unto the Lord.” When we bring tithes, which is food, to Jerusalem, you give the tenth part that the Lord blessed you with, the seed of the land and the fruit of the tree that his rain brought forth. That tenth part is the mercy that he shows us, and it is holy unto the Lord.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

points: A singular vow is a man binding himself to the Most High: promising that in exchange for a blessing he will give himself, or what is his, to the service of the Lord. The persons vowed were valued by the estimation of the priest.
Hannah is the example: in bitterness of soul she vowed that if the Lord gave her a man child she would give him unto the Lord all the days of his life, and that is how the story of Samuel began.

Christ taught on this because a vow is dangerous: you must pay your vow. Better not to swear at all, but let your communication be yea, yea; that is why we just say Lord's will, Lord's will I get this done.

The estimation is the value set for redeeming a person out of the vow. A male from twenty to sixty years old, the prime of life, was fifty shekels of silver after the shekel of the sanctuary, and a female thirty shekels.

From five years to twenty years old the male was twenty shekels and the female ten; from a month old to five years the male was five shekels and the female three; and from sixty years old and above the male was fifteen shekels and the female ten.

If the man was poorer than the estimation and could not pay it, he presented himself before the priest, and the priest valued him according to the ability of him that vowed, his worth and what he was able to bring forth.

If a beast was brought as an offering to the Most High it had to be holy, not blemished; it could not be altered or changed, a good for a bad or a bad for a good, and if it was changed at all, both it and the exchange became holy.

An unclean beast, one with a blemish that could not be sacrificed, was presented before the priest and the priest valued it, good or bad; and to redeem it, a fifth part had to be added to the estimation to get that beast back.
A man could sanctify his house to be holy unto the Most High, and the priest estimated it, good or bad, and as the priest estimated it, so it stood.

To redeem the house he added the fifth part of the money of the estimation: if the house was worth a hundred thousand, he paid that hundred thousand plus the extra twenty thousand, and it was his again.

A field sanctified to the Most High was estimated according to the seed thereof, an homer of barley seed at fifty shekels of silver; from the year of jubile the estimation stood full, but after the jubile the priest reckoned the money according to the years that remained, and it was abated from the estimation.

The jubile was the year of release, when the land had to rest, so the value was reckoned by how close the jubile was: the fewer years left to reap the field, the lower the estimation. It is like trading in a car; a two year old car with twenty thousand miles brings more value than an old car with a hundred and fifty thousand miles on it.

To redeem a sanctified field the fifth part was added to the estimation. A field not redeemed, or sold to another man, could not be redeemed any more, but went out in the jubile holy unto the Lord, a devoted field, the possession of the priest; and in the year of jubile a bought field returned to him of whom it was bought.
All the estimations were according to the shekel of the sanctuary, twenty gerahs to the shekel; that was the standard, the set price.

The firstling of the beasts could not be sanctified by any man, because as a firstling it was the Lord's already, whether ox or sheep; an unclean firstling was redeemed by the estimation with the fifth part added, or sold according to the estimation.

No devoted thing that a man devoted unto the Most High, of man, beast, or field of his possession, could be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the Lord, and a devoted man was surely put to death.
All the tithe of the land, of the seed of the land or the fruit of the tree, is the Lord's; it is holy unto the Lord. To redeem out of the tithes a man added the fifth part thereto.

The tithe of the herd and the flock, the tenth of whatsoever passeth under the rod, was holy unto the Lord; he was not to search whether it was good or bad or change it, and if he changed it at all, both it and the change were holy and could not be redeemed.
